recognition-is-evidence-of-attention.title: Recognition Is Evidence of Attention
recognition-is-evidence-of-attention.content:
Recognition Is Evidence of Attention
In a journal entry from 2021, I complained about the “constant noise of recognition.” I wrote that people build up a tolerance to praise and that we needed to become more precise and surgical about when and why we recognized someone.
I still think that is mostly right, although “surgical” sounds a little intense for saying thank you.
What I was reacting to was not recognition itself. It was recognition that had become detached from observation.
“Great job.”
“Amazing team.”
“Thank you for everything you do.”
All pleasant. Almost no information.
The person may feel appreciated for a moment, but they do not know what you saw. They do not know what mattered. After enough repetition, the praise becomes part of the wallpaper.
Precise recognition is operational feedback
Useful recognition usually contains three things:

What the person actually did
What was difficult or easy to miss about the situation
What became better because they did it

For example:

I noticed that you called the family before they had to ask for an update. You did it during a day when several other cases needed your attention. That kept them from spending the afternoon wondering whether anyone was working on their problem.

That is not only praise. It is information.
It tells the person that anticipation mattered. It tells the rest of the team, if the recognition is public, what kind of work the organization values. It gives the employee something concrete they can repeat.
This is why I have started thinking that recognition is evidence of attention.
It tells someone: I saw the work itself, not merely the result attached to your name.
A lot of important work is nearly invisible
Someone notices that a coworker is overloaded and quietly takes a task. An experienced employee catches a problem before it reaches a supervisor. A person gives honest feedback in a room where silence would have been easier. Someone brings steadiness into a difficult day and the emotional temperature of the whole team changes.
None of that is likely to appear on a dashboard.
If leaders recognize only the loudest wins, people learn that the quieter work does not count. Worse, leadership loses information about what is actually keeping the operation together.
This is related to the limits of formal metrics. What can be measured matters. What cannot be measured still exists.
Recognition can make some of that invisible work legible—but only if the leader is close enough to notice it.
The exercise changed when I asked why
Years later, I facilitated a gratitude discussion with a leadership team. The ground rule was specificity: something from the last 30 days, large or small, whether the person knew they had done it or not.
The first answer was rarely the interesting part. The useful part came from asking:

Why did that stay with you?
What would have happened if they had not done it?
What made the moment meaningful?
What, specifically, did they do?

Those questions turned compliments into a description of how the team functioned.
People talked about reliability under pressure, anticipation, honest feedback, energy, trust, and the small things that make difficult work sustainable. None of it was heroic. That was the point.
The operation was being held together by consistent acts of attention.
Recognition without the gaps becomes performance
The gratitude discussion became more useful when we turned the lens around and asked where leadership had created extra burden, uncertainty, or silence for somebody else.
I went first.
That part matters to me because recognition can become another leadership ritual where leaders perform warmth without becoming more accountable to the work. If I am willing to tell someone exactly what they did that helped, I should also be willing to hear exactly what I did that made their job harder.
Recognition and accountability are not opposites. Both begin with noticing accurately and being specific enough that another person can act on what you noticed.
That is also why praise should not be used as a cushion around feedback. People can feel when the compliment is merely the bread in a criticism sandwich. Say what was good because it was good. Say what needs to change because it needs to change. Give both the dignity of precision.
Public or private?
Not every recognition should happen in front of the team.
Some people enjoy public attention. Some hate it. Some contributions involve details that should remain private. Sometimes the most meaningful version is a quiet sentence after a difficult shift: I saw what you did there. It mattered.
The goal is not visibility for its own sake. The goal is for the person to know that the work was seen and understood.
This is one reason recognition belongs beside hard conversations and debriefing in my head. All three depend on a leader paying close enough attention to describe reality without making the conversation about themselves.
What I am still trying to understand
Recognition can make hidden work visible. It can also accidentally reward people for continuing to absorb work the system should fix.
If I repeatedly praise the person who stays late to rescue a broken process, am I recognizing commitment—or teaching the organization to depend on their sacrifice?
I do not think the answer is to withhold recognition. I think the answer is to let the recognition produce a second question:

Why did this require someone to step up in the first place?

That question links recognition back to system design. See the person. Thank them precisely. Then pay attention to what their effort is telling you about the operation.
Connected notes

Leadership Philosophy — trust, warmth, and the emotional temperature of a team
Hard Conversations — feedback with dignity and specificity
The Debrief — paying attention without taking over the person’s experience
Build the Sprinkler System — when admirable effort is concealing a preventable gap

stop-being-the-answer.title: Stop Being the Answer
stop-being-the-answer.content:
Stop Being the Answer
One of the things I was really good at as a supervisor was answering questions.
Which, looking back, might have been a problem.
I knew the operation. I knew the policies. I had usually dealt with some version of whatever was being brought to me, and—if I am being completely honest—I liked being the person people came to. It feels good to be useful. It feels like leadership when someone brings you a problem and you can make it disappear.
But every time I gave someone an answer, I was also teaching them something.
Sometimes I was teaching them how to think through the problem. Sometimes I was teaching them to come back to me the next time it happened.
Those can look exactly the same in the moment.
Expertise creates a strange trap
You usually become a supervisor because you were good at the work. Then you spend a surprising amount of your time proving that you are still good at it.
The clinical question comes to you. The policy question comes to you. The schedule exception, the difficult customer, the unusual call, the employee who is not sure whether they are allowed to make the obvious decision—all of it comes to you. You answer quickly because you can, which reinforces the idea that bringing it to you was the correct move.
Eventually you become a permission queue.
The operation may even look efficient while this is happening. Decisions are getting made. Problems are getting solved. You are busy all day and everybody can point to how much you handle.
Then you take a day off.
The real measure of supervisory work has always been what happens when you are not there. That idea is already inside my leadership philosophy, but I do not think I understood all of its implications at first. Making yourself unnecessary is not only about training people well. It is also about noticing the ways your own usefulness has become part of the system’s design.
Not every question is the same question
I do not think the answer is to become the annoying manager who responds to everything with “What do you think?”
There are times when someone needs an answer. There are decisions they should not have to make alone. Sometimes the information is genuinely held at another level. Sometimes policy or law fixes the boundary. Sometimes a question is really an employee saying, “I need you to own this risk with me.”
That is not necessarily dependence. It may be good judgment.
But there are also questions that reach a supervisor because nobody has ever made it clear that the employee is allowed to answer them.
That is a different problem.
I started thinking about what would happen if a supervisor logged every question that reached them for two weeks. Nothing complicated: what was asked, how risky it actually was, whether it had come up before, and whether the person could reasonably have decided without you.
I suspect patterns would become obvious very quickly.
You might find an experienced employee asking permission for a routine schedule change. You might find that every complaint escalates because nobody knows where their authority ends. You might find ten slightly different questions that are all actually the same missing process. Or you might learn that the team is escalating appropriately because leadership has not given them access to what they need.
The point is not to reduce the number of questions as if questions are waste. The point is to understand what the questions reveal.
Authority has to move with responsibility
“Use your judgment” sounds empowering. It can also leave a person completely exposed.
If a team member is responsible for an outcome but has to return to you for every meaningful decision, they do not own the outcome. You do. You have simply added another person to the communication chain.
Real delegation includes a boundary:

You can decide this independently.
You can decide it, then tell me.
Bring me a recommendation before you act.
Stop and escalate before doing anything.

The categories are not profound. Making them explicit is.
I would start with the five most frequent, lowest-risk decisions. Not because small decisions are the most important, but because they are somewhere safe to practice moving authority. As judgment grows, the boundary can move.
The person should know what they can decide, what kind of risk changes the answer, and whether leadership will support a reasonable decision that did not produce the hoped-for outcome.
That last part matters. If the first imperfect decision causes you to seize the authority back, the original delegation was theater.
The answer is not to disappear
There is a version of “empowerment” that is really just leadership refusing to help.
Handing someone a problem without context, authority, or support and telling them to own it is not development. It is abandonment with better vocabulary.
I am still trying to locate the line between helping someone develop judgment and making them feel alone with a decision they were not prepared to make. I think the line moves by person, by risk, and sometimes by day. Someone can be completely capable and still need a second brain after a difficult shift.
Maybe the work is not to stop answering questions. Maybe it is to become more deliberate about what an answer is doing.
Is it transferring knowledge? Sharing risk? Clarifying a boundary? Or quietly keeping you at the center of the operation?
That is the question I wish I had asked more often.
Connected notes

Leadership Philosophy — the broader idea of leading through questions
The Debrief — helping someone recover and trust their own judgment
A Problem Passed Around Is a Problem Owned by Nobody — why distributing work is not the same as assigning ownership
Where does empowerment end and abandonment begin? — the edge I have not resolved

the-debrief.title: The Debrief
the-debrief.content:
The Debrief
The debrief is the most underused tool in EMS leadership. Most supervisors skip it, rush it, or do it wrong. Done right, it’s the fastest way to build crew confidence and catch problems before they become patterns.

What It’s Actually For
The instinct is to treat a debrief as a performance review — what went wrong, what needs to improve. That’s not what this is.
The debrief is for the crew member. Not for you, not for documentation, not for risk management. For them.
The goal is simple: leave the conversation with the crew member feeling more capable than when they entered it. Nine times out of ten, the thing they’re spiraling about — the call they keep replaying, the decision they’re second-guessing — comes down to one thing: they already had the skills and knowledge to handle it. They just didn’t trust themselves in the moment.
Your job is to help them find that.

The Method: Lead, Don’t Tell
Borrowed from the question-led model in Leadership Philosophy, but applied to crew support:
My default was not to give the answer first.
Instead:


Open with curiosity, not evaluation. “Walk me through that call.” Not “what did you do wrong.”


Ask what they were thinking in the moment. “What were you working with when you made that decision?” This surfaces their internal reasoning without judgment.


Ask what they’d look for next time. “If that came in again tomorrow, what would you want to pay attention to?” This is forward-facing without implying they failed.


Reflect their competence back. “You had the right instinct. You were already doing the assessment. What you’re describing is exactly what good clinical thinking sounds like.”


Close with what they can carry forward. One concrete thing. Not a list.


The crew member should be doing most of the talking. If you’re doing most of the talking, you’re not debriefing — you’re lecturing.

Timing Matters
Hot debriefs (immediately post-call) are for acute stress. Keep them short, normalize the emotional response, don’t go clinical yet.
Cold debriefs (hours later, next shift) are where the learning happens. Give people time to process before asking them to reflect analytically.
Not every call needs both. Not every call needs a formal debrief at all. The signal that one is needed: the crew member is still carrying it.

The Calls That Require Extra Care
Pediatric calls. Traumatic deaths. Calls where things went wrong and the outcome was bad regardless of what the crew did.
For these, the clinical debrief comes second. First: normalize that this was hard, that the response they’re having is appropriate, that it means they care. Then — and only then — if they want to talk through the clinical — go there.
After a call that ended badly, I would not lead with “here is what you should have done differently.” Even when the feedback is true and necessary, the timing can bury it.

What I Noticed Over Years of This
My observation was that crews who were regularly debriefed—not punished, actually debriefed—became more reflective over time. They began talking through calls with one another without waiting for a supervisor to initiate it.
I did not run a controlled study of whether those crews made fewer errors. I believed they did, and the mechanism made sense to me, but that is a retrospective operational judgment rather than a measured result. The part I can state more confidently is that the habit began to move from the supervisor into the crew.
That’s the goal. Make yourself unnecessary.
A debrief is not an investigation or therapy
These boundaries matter.
A supportive debrief can help someone process a difficult call and recover their reasoning. It does not replace professional mental-health support when that is what the person needs. It also does not replace a formal investigation when patient care, policy, safety, or misconduct requires one.
The conversations may connect. Their purposes are different.
That is the same distinction I am trying to preserve in The Report Was Accurate. It Was Still Incomplete. A conversation can reveal context a formal record did not carry. More context does not erase the need for process, evidence, or accountable review.

Related

Leadership Philosophy — the mindset behind this approach
Training FTOs — how to teach FTOs to run debriefs
Hard Conversations — when the conversation isn’t about the call
The Report Was Accurate. It Was Still Incomplete. — how conversation and formal records serve different purposes
Stop Being the Answer — the tension between helping and taking over

The prompts are embedded in the Provider Development Review tools. The same question-led instinct influenced chatIR, although a product-supported incident conversation and a human debrief are not interchangeable.

tools.title: Field Tools
tools.content:
Field Tools
Seven printable tools — one for each major challenge in EMS supervision. Each one is built around the frameworks in this garden, not borrowed from somewhere else.
All seven are included in the EMS Supervisor Field Guide — free with your email on Gumroad.

Investigation & Safety
Tool 01 — Vehicle Accident Investigation Form
The SPECS framework on paper. For each incident: Scene, Process & Policy, Equipment & Load, Crew, System. Causal-chain drill. Contributing conditions. System recommendations first, operator coaching where supported. The form is built around one premise: the individual operator is usually the last link in a much longer causal chain. Companion to Fleet Safety and The Report Was Accurate. It Was Still Incomplete..
Tool 02 — Incident Findings Report
The formal write-up after an investigation is complete. Timeline, SPECS findings summary, conclusion, recommendations. Designed to be read by someone who wasn’t there. Pairs with Tool 01.

Provider Development
Tool 03 — Provider Development Review, Phase 1
Monthly coaching log for providers in a development program. Attendance and documentation tracked against clear thresholds, but the core is a coaching log with the debrief prompts embedded — so an FTO using this form has the methodology right in front of them. Skills tracked on a See / Do / Teach progression. Companion to Training FTOs.
Tool 04 — Provider Development Review, Phase 2
Same structure as Phase 1, higher bar: zero addenda target, On Scene Times coaching added, final advancement recommendation. The Independence Check section asks the question that matters: what can this provider do without you now?

Leadership
Tool 05 — Performance Conversation Record
Documents a performance conversation. Four severity levels from coaching through final warning. Structured around what was observed, what was said, and what changes going forward. Not a substitute for the conversation—a record of one that already happened. Companion to Hard Conversations and Recognition Is Evidence of Attention.
Tool 07 — Supervisor Self-Evaluation
Quarterly self-assessment mapped to five areas: leading versus answering, debrief quality, hard-conversation timing, metrics, and crew independence. Ends with one commitment for the next 90 days. Companion to Leadership Philosophy and Stop Being the Answer.
Tool 08 — FTO Selection Guide
Behavioral interview guide for selecting FTO candidates. Five questions targeting teaching ability, handling a struggling trainee, productive struggle, running debriefs, and consistency under pressure. Scoring rubric built around what the trainee gets out of the partnership — not what the FTO demonstrates. Companion to Training FTOs.



                  
                  Get all seven in one place 
                  
                

The EMS Supervisor Field Guide collects all seven tools plus the full methodology — 43 pages, free with your email on Gumroad.

training-ftos.title: Training FTOs
training-ftos.content:
Training FTOs
Training a field training officer is different from training an EMT. You’re not teaching clinical skills — you’re teaching someone how to teach. That’s a harder thing to do, and almost nobody does it deliberately.
I trained 30+ people at Royal Ambulance over my time as an FTO and supervisor. Here’s what I learned.

The Core Problem
Most FTOs were selected because they were excellent clinicians. That’s necessary but not sufficient. Being good at a job does not automatically make you good at explaining it to someone who isn’t.
The trap new FTOs fall into: they demonstrate instead of develop. They show the trainee how to do the skill, the trainee watches, and everyone moves on. No learning has actually occurred. What’s occurred is observation.
The goal isn’t for your trainee to have watched you do the thing. It’s for your trainee to be able to do the thing when you’re not there.
That is the same identity shift a new supervisor faces in Stop Being the Answer. Your competence is still necessary. It simply stops being the product. The other person’s judgment is the product now.

Teaching FTOs to Teach
When I trained FTOs, or mentored them through training questions, the through-line was always the same: shift from demonstrating to developing.
Practical framework — see one, do one, teach one:
1. See one. They watch. Once, maybe twice. Before you start, tell them what to pay attention to — not a running commentary during. Let them observe without narration cluttering it.
2. Do one. Trainee attempts. Before you hand it over, narrate your reasoning out loud — not the steps, the thinking. “I’m starting here because… I’m checking this because…” Most experienced providers have automated their reasoning. Making it explicit again takes practice. Then step back and let them work. Resist the urge to jump in.
3. Teach one. They can walk someone else through it. That’s the real test. Not whether they can execute — whether they understand it well enough to explain the why. If they can’t teach it, they don’t own it yet.
Debrief after every attempt. Not a list of corrections — use the Socratic method. See The Debrief. “What were you working with when you made that decision? What would you pay attention to next time?”
Move through the progression as fast as the trainee can handle. The FTO’s job is to become unnecessary.

Common FTO Mistakes
Rescuing too early. The trainee pauses, the FTO steps in. Natural instinct, wrong move. Productive struggle is where learning happens. Let them sit in it a little longer than feels comfortable.
Correcting in front of the patient. If immediate safety requires intervention, intervene. Otherwise, pull them aside afterward. The debrief is private. The call is not the time for a performance review.
Inconsistency. Different standards on different shifts, depending on how the FTO feels that day. Trainees notice immediately and it destroys trust. Consistent doesn’t mean rigid — it means your trainees know what to expect from you.
Skipping the “why.” Teaching steps without teaching reasoning can produce a trainee who performs in familiar scenarios and struggles when the shape changes. Teach the “why.” EMS is too unpredictable for rote execution alone.
A completion record can show that the trainee received the material. It cannot, by itself, show that the trainee can recognize the situation, adapt, and perform under pressure. I am still trying to find better ways to make that difference visible without turning development into another pile of checkboxes.

The Hygiene Problem (And All the Other Uncomfortable Ones)
New FTOs ask about this more than almost anything else. “My trainee doesn’t use deodorant. How do I handle it?”
Directly. Privately. Kindly. Quickly.
The longer you wait, the harder it gets, and the more it affects the partnership. These conversations feel enormous beforehand and are usually over in three minutes. The formula: private setting, specific observation, no editorializing, clear expectation, move on.
The same framework applies to almost every uncomfortable FTO conversation. Don’t build up to it, don’t over-explain, don’t apologize for having the conversation. Have it and be done with it.

What Makes a Good FTO, Honestly
Clinical competence — yes, required.
Patience — more than you think you have.
Genuine investment in the trainee’s success — not their performance on your watch, their success in the career. Those are different things.
The ability to remember what it was like to not know something. This gets harder the more experienced you become. Fight to hold onto it.

Related

The Debrief — the most important FTO skill
Leadership Philosophy — the mindset underneath all of this
Hard Conversations — the uncomfortable stuff FTOs face
Stop Being the Answer — resisting the urge to make your expertise the center of the learning

The Provider Development Reviews and FTO Selection Guide are the practical companions to this note.
